Elasticsearch

Source: vignettes/elasticsearch.Rmd
elasticsearch.Rmd

Use oauth_db_elasticsearch_api() to search documents or run SQL and ES|QL with each Shiny visitor’s access token. Elasticsearch checks the token and applies that user’s roles, including document and field restrictions. The client uses HTTPS and needs jsonlite, without a database driver.

This guide uses an external identity provider and an Elasticsearch JWT realm configured for access tokens. It supports self-managed Elasticsearch and Elastic Cloud Hosted deployments with that realm enabled. Check your subscription for JWT realm availability. Elastic Cloud Serverless does not support authentication realms, so this setup does not apply to Serverless.

Configure the deployment

Ask your Elasticsearch administrator to configure a JWT realm accepting the access tokens issued to your app. The access_token realm type requires Elasticsearch 8.7 or later. Configure the issuer, audience, signing keys, allowed subjects and claims used for the username and groups.

For example, a realm named visitors in elasticsearch.yml could contain:

xpack.security.authc.realms.jwt.visitors:
  order: 0
  token_type: access_token
  client_authentication.type: shared_secret
  allowed_issuer: "https://login.example.org/realms/reporting"
  allowed_audiences: ["elasticsearch-reporting"]
  allowed_subjects: ["alice-subject", "bob-subject"]
  allowed_signature_algorithms: ["RS256"]
  pkc_jwkset_path: "https://login.example.org/realms/reporting/protocol/openid-connect/certs"
  claims.principal: sub
  claims.groups: groups

Replace the subjects with the provider’s actual sub values, or configure appropriate allowed_subject_patterns. The provider must issue JWT access tokens containing iss, aud, sub, iat and exp; opaque tokens won’t work with this realm. Configure the audience for the data service, and keep ID tokens separate from access tokens.

Store the application’s realm shared secret in the Elasticsearch keystore:

bin/elasticsearch-keystore add xpack.security.authc.realms.jwt.visitors.client_authentication.shared_secret

For Elastic Cloud Hosted, use the deployment’s configuration and secure settings controls. The Shiny app needs the same realm shared secret. This secret authenticates the application and is separate from the secret used by shinyOAuth for the OAuth client registration.

Create Elasticsearch roles and role mappings for your users. For example, an administrator could grant a provider group named analysts read access:

PUT /_security/role/orders_reader
{
  "indices": [{
    "names": ["orders"],
    "privileges": ["read", "view_index_metadata"]
  }]
}

PUT /_security/role_mapping/reporting_analysts
{
  "enabled": true,
  "roles": ["orders_reader"],
  "rules": {"all": [
    {"field": {"realm.name": "visitors"}},
    {"field": {"groups": "analysts"}}
  ]}
}

Add document and field restrictions to those roles when users should see different records or fields. OAuth scopes requested by the app do not grant Elasticsearch index privileges. Configuring Kibana’s OIDC login also does not configure this JWT realm for API requests.

See Elastic’s JWT realm guide and Serverless authentication limitations.

Register your app and save its settings

Register a Shiny web application with the identity provider trusted by the realm. Use http://localhost:8100 as its redirect URI for this example. The provider must issue access tokens for the configured Elasticsearch audience and include the user or group claims needed by your role mappings.

Save these settings in .Renviron and restart R:

Setting Value
OAUTHDB_ELASTICSEARCH_URL Deployment HTTPS URL, without /_search or /_sql
OAUTHDB_ELASTICSEARCH_ISSUER Identity provider issuer URL
OAUTHDB_ELASTICSEARCH_REALM_SECRET Shared secret configured for the JWT realm
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID, OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET OAuth registration’s ID and secret

The example requests search.read, a scope your provider must define or replace. Configure the token audience with your provider’s settings. If it needs an authorization parameter such as Auth0’s audience, pass it through the provider’s extra_auth_params; an arbitrary scope name won’t set it. See Getting started for registration and token settings.

A complete app

Replace orders and the requested scope with those used by your deployment. The realm’s user role must permit reading the index.

After signing in, click Load rows. The app starts its workers once and stops them at shutdown.

library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(
  issuer = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ELASTICSEARCH_ISSUER")
)

client <- oauth_client(
  provider,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile", "search.read")
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),

    actionButton("load", "Load rows"),
    verbatimTextOutput("rows")
  ),

  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

fetch_rows <- function(database) {
  database$database(
    "orders",
    body = list(size = 20L, query = list(term = list(country = "NL")))
  )$hits
}

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server(
    "auth",
    client,
    auto_redirect = FALSE,
    async = TRUE
  )

  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  search <- oauth_db_elasticsearch_api(
    auth$connection,
    url = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ELASTICSEARCH_URL"),
    client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_ELASTICSEARCH_REALM_SECRET"),
    required_scopes = "search.read"
  )

  query_task <- oauth_db_task(search, method = fetch_rows)

  observeEvent(input$load, {
    query_task$invoke()
  })

  output$rows <- renderPrint(query_task$result())
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*", onStart = function() {
    mirai::daemons(2)

    onStop(function() mirai::daemons(0))
  }),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

# Open the app in your regular browser at its registered redirect URI.

Open http://localhost:8100 in your regular browser. For a private CA, pass its PEM bundle through ca_bundle when creating the API client.

SQL, ES|QL and pagination

SQL and ES|QL return their native column metadata and rows as lists. Large JSON integers remain strings and multivalued fields remain nested lists. Bind parameter values separately from the query:

sql <- search$sql(
  "SELECT country, total FROM orders WHERE country = ?",
  parameters = list("NL")
)

sql$columns
sql$rows

esql <- search$esql(
  "FROM orders | WHERE country == ? | KEEP country, total | LIMIT 20",
  parameters = list("NL")
)

esql$values

ES|QL and its parameter syntax depend on the server version. The integration check uses Elasticsearch 9.2.0. For named ES|QL parameters or other native options, use $request() with the server’s JSON body format.

The client returns one page per call. Fetch search pages explicitly using search_after and a stable sort. For SQL, use the returned cursor:

if (!is.null(sql$cursor)) {
  page <- search$request(
    "_sql",
    method = "POST",
    body = list(cursor = sql$cursor)
  )

  if (!is.null(page$cursor)) {
    search$request(
      c("_sql", "close"),
      method = "POST",
      body = list(cursor = page$cursor)
    )
  }
}

SQL column metadata appears on the first page only. Keep cursors and point-in-time identifiers with the authorization that created them; consume or close them before changing accounts and discard saved identifiers after sign-out. There is no automatic pagination or cursor cleanup.

Each call gets a current token. The client discards responses if the user signs out, switches accounts or loses required scopes during a request. GET and HEAD can refresh and retry once after a 401. POST searches, SQL, ES|QL and writes never retry automatically, including after a 401 or a lost response. Submitted work may continue on the server after a client timeout.

Search timeouts, failed shards and partial query results raise errors. Use raw = TRUE to inspect the HTTP response, or $request() when you need to handle native response metadata yourself. The client supports JSON APIs; bulk NDJSON requests need a different client.
